problem: Existing language-guided navigation and semantic SLAM systems rely on depth sensors (RGB-D/LiDAR/IMU), offline processing, fine-tuned models or shallow CLIP-style semantics, which limits deployment on lightweight monocular robots.
motivation: Service and assistive robots need low-cost, RGB-only platforms that still understand open-vocabulary language. MASt3R-SLAM makes real-time dense monocular mapping feasible, but has no semantics or language interface, so pairing it with off-the-shelf VLMs is a natural route.
key_idea: Combine monocular MASt3R-SLAM dense mapping with off-the-shelf VLMs (Gemma 3, Qwen2.5-VL) run on keyframes to annotate the 3D map, then retrieve language-specified goals and plan paths with Dijkstra/A*.
insight: The paper is a system-integration study, so the takeaways are latency and quality trade-offs, not navigation performance. Detailed prompts and larger VLMs greatly increase latency (Gemma-3-4B short 0.52 s vs Qwen2.5-7B detailed 5.27 s, Table II), and offline mapping gives ~2.8x denser point clouds than real-time (40,492 vs 14,663 pts/m³, Table III) at lower FPS. The language-guided goal retrieval and planning are not quantitatively evaluated.
method: Dense monocular mapping: MASt3R-SLAM gives pointmap regression, learned matching, second-order pose-graph optimization with loop closure, and dense maps from RGB only.
Keyframe-centric semantic annotation: Gemma 3 or Qwen2.5-VL is run only on selected keyframes to give open-vocabulary labels, attributes and grounding, cutting compute.
Semantic projection: image-region semantics are projected onto keyframe map points and incrementally updated in the global 3D map.

Language goal retrieval: the instruction is parsed for intent, objects and attributes; text embeddings are matched to map semantics by similarity, then refined with semantic consistency and 3D geometric checks.
Path planning: a collision-free path to the goal is computed with graph-based planners (Dijkstra/A*); closed-loop control is left for future work.
Prompt styles: short (object names only) versus detailed (attributes and spatial context) prompts, both capped at 256 tokens.

setting.action_space: planned path on the map (Dijkstra/A*); no closed-loop low-level control evaluated

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark results (SR/SPL etc.) are reported; only VLM latency (Table II) and mapping density/FPS (Table III), which do not fit the navigation metrics.
results: The system builds dense monocular maps and produces open-vocabulary labels in sim and on a real TurtleBot3. Latency of the first token ranges from 0.52 s (Gemma-3-4B, short prompt) to 5.27 s (Qwen2.5-7B, detailed prompt). Offline mapping reaches 40,492 pts/m³ at 4.0 FPS versus 14,663 pts/m³ at ~5-6 FPS for real-time mode. There are no baseline comparisons or task success metrics.
limitations: No quantitative navigation evaluation (no success rate, no baselines); goal retrieval and planning are only described, closed-loop planning is future work.
VLM latency (0.5-5 s) and a heavy workstation (RTX 4090) limit real-time and embedded use; evaluation is qualitative and small-scale, with no systematic language-query tests.
